McKinsey.org 11
Setting meaningful learning intentions
Adaptability & Resilience 
Setting learning intentions
Tip: to set meaningful learning
intentions, follow these 3 guiding
principles to ensure you get the
most out of setting these intentions
1. Preparation: investing the time and energy to
set yourself up for success
2. Execution: learning and performing to the best
of your capabilities, and enjoying yourself in
the process
3. Reflection: learning from your past actions
Focus on the journey
Frame your desired outcome as a learning intention 
versus a performance goal.
Good learning intentions prioritize the experience 
itself, not just the outcome. Instead of focusing on a 
specific target, they focus on:
 The process
 Discovering and exploring new ideas
 Our growth
Link to meaning
Connect your learning to something that is
personally meaningful to you.
Takingthe time to make this connection
will help you learn better and have more fun in
the process.
Questions you might ask yourself include:
 When things get hard, what keeps me motivated?
 What makes me feel fulfilled and proud?
My notes
We live in a complex world with more stimuli than we can possibly process. Setting learning intentions
helps us to cut through the noise and stay focused on what we’ve identified as personally important.
There are two specific, subtle ways in which we can frame our intentions—our direction forward—that
support both our ability to learn and the likelihood that we’ll enjoy the experience.

Turning behaviors into habits
What’s the reminder?
In other words, what cue will trigger
your habit?
You might set an electronic reminder: for
example, a calendar invite that pops up at
the start of every week.
You might try a physical note or object, like
a reminder you place by your desk. Or
perhaps you have a calendar out in the
open, featuring an X on every day that you 
gave or received feedback.
What will your reward be? What
will make you feel good about
your routine?
When adopting feedback as a learning
habit, the feedbackitself can be the reward.
But you should also consider other physical,
mental, or emotional rewards.
The reward could be the gratification of
marking a big X on your calendar or
somethingmore concrete.
What’s the routine?
What steps are required to uphold
this habit?

Adaptability and Resilience Key Takeaways
Adaptability & Resilience
Learning Intention vs. PerformanceGoal:
Set a learning intention when acquiring a new skill; use
performance goals when you already have the skills and want to
achieve specific results.
Mindset awareness:
Differentiate between your helpful and unhelpful mindsets and 
recognize their influence on your behavior and progress.
Focus on the journey and personal meaning:
Improve your ability to learn by focusing on the process, not
just the outcome, and connect your learning to something 
personally meaningful.
Shift Mindsets for Resilience:
Cultivate adaptability and resilience by practicingAPR 
(Awareness,Pause, and Reframe) during challenging situations.
Habit Formation:
Develop a customized action plan for building desired habits
and unlearning unhealthy ones. Utilize the habit loop (Cue,
Routine, Reward) to reinforce positive habits effectively.

Testing your problem definition using the SMART framework
Is the question specific enough? Your problem question needs to be
detailed enough so that those who are closest to the problem can
understand the exact problem that needs to be solved.
Specific
The problem question should point to the action that needs to be done
to solve the problem. Usually, you will need to use the language
"How?" or "What actions do we need to take?" in your problem question.
Actionable
Your problem question should be relevant to everyone involved in the
situation: the executive, your team, and any other stakeholders. It's 
important to align everyone so that you all have same goals in mind.
Relevant
Problem questions should always be time bound to ensure that
everyone comes up with solutions that are practical in the time frame
that you have defined.
Time-bound

Using a Problem Statement Worksheet to define a problem
Stakeholders
List all the major players critical to your solution.
Consider all decision makers who could support—or
block—your solution. Also include internal or external 
parties who might affect how your solution is
implemented.
Scope of solution space
What will and will not be consideredin your
solution? The scope should be broad enough to
ensure that you’re consideringall relevant
solutions, yet narrow enough to ensure that your 
analysis is manageable.
Constraints within solution space
While scope defines the space of your solution,
constraintsfocus on what can or cannot happen
within that space.
Context
Think about the “environment”around the problem
you’re facing. Will internal or external situations
affect how you solve the problem? Are there 
complications to consider? This field may
encompasscurrent industry trends, availabilityof
finances, or skill gaps on your team.
Key sources of insight
These are where you will turn for information. Can
you leverage available resources from your
department,company, or industry?
Identifying these resources will simplify your effort
and ensure you’re not repeating work that’s already
been done.
Criteria for success
What must happen for your solution to be 
successful?What could happen to make your 
solution a failure? Consider timing of impact, visibility 
of improvement,mindset shifts, and what success
looks like for key stakeholders. Criteria should be
measurable,so you can judge whether or not your
final solution satisfies them.
Problem Solving
​ Defining the problem
Problem question (The basic question to be resolved)
Concisely define, in the form of a question, what must be resolved. This focuses your work and ensures that your findings are actionable. 
Your basic question should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Action-oriented, Relevant, and Time-bound
Tip: Use this to summarize the problem in a concise way, 
clarifying precisely what needs solving.

What should the pyramid contain?
 A single governing thought which is the key takeaway
the audience must hear during the first 2 minutes of
your communication event.
 3-5 key line statements that act as the underlying
arguments that support the governing thought.
 3-5 supporting facts per key line statement which build
the foundation of your pyramid and support both the
key line statements and the governing thought.
 Mutually exclusive: The groups address unique issues with no overlap.
 Collectively exhaustive: As a set, the groups represent the spectrum of issues
at play, leaving no gaps.

takeaways and next steps with owners and deadlines.

Principles for putting this into practice
No matter which source of well-being you want to prioritize, or the specific behaviors you want to 
improve, there are four big ideas that will help you maximize your efforts.
 Tiny behaviors lead to sustainable change: be specific and focused in your actions.
 Small and frequent is best: don’t rely on just one big moment to energize yourself.
 You have positive habits you can build upon: identify some existing cues that prompt healthy
behaviors.
 People matter: find others who can support you, offer feedback, and share ideas with you.
Your well-being tank is fueled by four sources: mental, physical, social, and spiritual. However, our habits often cause us to 
prioritize just one or two of these sources.
To ensure your well-being is truly at its best, you should consider all four.

MILAN 26
LITERARY CLUB
EVENT NAME: Shipwreck
TEAM SIZE: Solo
DESCRIPTION:
Each participant is assigned a character or object (e.g., a famous personality, an item, or a
fictional character) and must justify why they deserve to be saved and allowed on the
lifeboat over others.
RULES & REGULATIONS:
 10 minutes time of preparation time will be provided.
 Participants are allowed to use cell phones during the preparation time.
 No offensive language to be used.
 Responses must be quick-witted.
 Marks will be deducted based on stammering.
 The languages allowed are only english.
JUDGEMENT CRITERIA:
 Stage presence
 Vocal command
 Fluency in speaking
 Arguments must be logical
 Creative and Entertaining
 Adherence to the time limit

MILAN 26
LITERARY CLUB
EVENT NAME: Slam Poetry
TEAM SIZE: Solo
DESCRIPTION:
Participants have to write a poem on spot on the given prompt and recite it with passion,
emotion and expression.
RULES & REGULATIONS:
 25 minutes time for preparation (including writing) will be given.
 Any form of plagiarism will not be entertained.
 Points will be deducted for stuttering.
 Use of cell phones will not be allowed.
 Use of offensive language/content will not be tolerated and result in reduction in
points or disqualification.
 The languages allowed are only english.
JUDGEMENT CRITERIA:
 Authenticity of the poem
 Stage presence
 Usage of literary devices
 Rhythmic pattern (except in free verse poetry)
 Ability to connect with the audience

MILAN 26
LITERARY CLUB
EVENT NAME: DEBATE
TEAM SIZE: 3 in each team
DESCRIPTION:
A 3 vs 3 debate is a structured argumentation format where two teams, each consisting of
three members, compete against each other. One team takes the affirmative (for the motion)
side, while the other takes the negative (against the motion) side. Each speaker presents
arguments, rebuts opposing points, and defends their stance using logical reasoning, facts,
and persuasive speech.
RULES & REGULATIONS:
 1 hour time for preparation will be given before starting the debate.
 No time will be given in between rounds.
 Rebuttal Rounds:
o Exact number of rounds will be specified by the judge.
o First speaker speaks for 1 minute.
o 30 seconds for counter-questioning will be given to one of the members of the
opponent team.
o 30 seconds for the previous speaker to answer back.
 Use of offensive language/content will not be tolerated and result in reduction in
points or disqualification.
 Points will be deducted for stuttering.
 The languages allowed are only english.
JUDGEMENT CRITERIA:
 Vocal command
 Vocal strength
 Logic and Relevance of arguments (arguments should be factual)
 Use of evidence and examples
 Presentation and Delivery (body language and fluency while speaking)
 Team coordination
 Time management

MILAN 26
LITERARY CLUB
EVENT NAME: JAM
JUST A MINUTE
TEAM SIZE: Solo
DESCRIPTION:
Just A Minute (JAM) is a fun and challenging impromptu speaking event where participants
must speak continuously on a given topic for exactly one minute without hesitation,
repetition, or deviation.
TIME LIMIT: 1 minute
RULES & REGULATIONS:
 No preparation time will be given (15 seconds at most might be given).
 Participants must speak continuously for one minute without hesitation.
 Points will be deducted for stuttering.
 Repetition of any word or deviation from the given topic will lead to reduction in
points.
 Use of offensive language will not be tolerated and result in reduction in points or
disqualification.
 The languages allowed are only english.
JUDGEMENT CRITERIA:
 Vocal command
 Ability to speak smoothly
 Relevance to the topic
 Grammatical accuracy
 Vocabulary
